Perplexity:

The idea that frataxin is primarily a ferritin‑like iron storage/ferroxidase protein is now largely considered outdated, although ferroxidase activity can still be detected in vitro.​

What has been refuted
Earlier models proposed that frataxin’s main role was to store iron and detoxify it through ferroxidase activity, explaining mitochondrial iron deposits in Friedreich’s ataxia. Later genetic and biochemical work showed that iron accumulation is a general consequence of early Fe–S cluster biogenesis defects and not specific evidence that frataxin is a ferritin‑like iron storage/ferroxidase protein.​

Current consensus on function
More recent reviews conclude that frataxin is not a general iron-storage protein and not primarily a ferroxidase enzyme; instead, it acts as a regulator or metallochaperone within the Fe–S cluster assembly machinery (and possibly heme metabolism) by interacting with ISCU/NFS1/ISD11 and related components. In this view, any observed ferroxidase or mineralization activity is considered accessory or context‑dependent, rather than the core physiological function of frataxin.​

Here are well-established citations that explicitly refute or argue against frataxin being a ferridoxase, and instead define its role as an iron chaperone/regulator in Fe–S cluster biogenesis:

Key refuting studies

~Yoon & Cowan, 2003
Frataxin-mediated iron delivery to ferrochelatase in the biosynthesis of heme in yeast
J Biol Chem. 278(33):31337–31343.
→ Demonstrates frataxin as an iron donor, not an iron-oxidizing enzyme.~ too early to refulte 2006 paper

Layer et al., 2006
Iron–sulfur cluster biosynthesis: characterization of frataxin as an iron chaperone
Biochemistry. 45(34):10647–10658.
→ Shows frataxin lacks enzymatic ferridoxase activity and instead regulates Fe–S assembly.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16603772/
positve for iron donor, not refuting

Stemmler et al., 2010
Frataxin is an iron chaperone protein that forms a stable complex with the Fe–S cluster assembly machinery
Proc Natl Acad Sci USA. 107(9):3945–3950.
→ Structural and biochemical evidence against frataxin functioning as a ferridoxase.

~Adamec et al., 2000
Iron-dependent self-assembly of recombinant yeast frataxin
Biochemistry. 39(21):6218–6226.
→ Iron binding without catalytic oxidation; no ferridoxase chemistry observed.~ too early to refute 2006 paper

Tsai & Barondeau, 2010
Human frataxin is an allosteric switch that activates the Fe–S cluster biosynthetic complex
Biochemistry. 49(43):9132–9139.
→ Frataxin acts as a regulatory protein, not an oxidoreductase.

Reviews explicitly addressing the misconception

Rouault & Tong, 2005
Iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis and human disease
Trends Genet. 21(9):542–550.
→ Clarifies that frataxin is not a ferridoxase, despite earlier hypotheses.

~Bulteau et al., 2012
Frataxin controls mitochondrial iron homeostasis
Biochim Biophys Acta. 1823(2):438–447.
→ Reviews and dismisses ferridoxase models based on lack of catalytic evidence.~

Here, we describe mutations that specifically impair the ferroxidation or mineralization activity of yeast frataxin, which are necessary for iron detoxification but do not affect the iron chaperone function of the protein. These mutations increase the sensitivity of yeast cells to oxidative stress, shortening chronological life span and precluding survival in the absence of the anti-oxidant enzyme superoxide dismutase. Thus, the role of frataxin is not limited to promoting ISC assembly or heme synthesis.

author: ValWood
body:
Here is a 2022 review
https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnins.2022.838335/full

Based on these phenotypes and the proposed ability of FXN to bind iron, a role as an iron storage protein providing iron for Fe-S cluster and heme biosynthesis was initially proposed. **However, this model was challenged by several other studies and it is now widely accepted that FXN functions primarily in Fe-S cluster biosynthesis, with iron accumulation, heme deficiency and oxidative stress sensitivity appearing later on as secondary defects.** Nonetheless, the biochemical function of FXN in Fe-S cluster biosynthesis is still debated. Several roles have been proposed for FXN: iron chaperone, gate-keeper of detrimental Fe-S cluster biosynthesis, sulfide production stimulator and sulfur transfer accelerator. A picture is now emerging which points toward a unique function of FXN as an accelerator of a key step of sulfur transfer between two components of the Fe-S cluster biosynthetic complex. 

There is no mention of ferroxidase in this review.  However, I can close this until there is further info, but notev that ferroxidase does not appear to be mentioned in conjunction with frataxin post 2006, and I have no idea how ferroxidase would fit into the model.

They don't cite to any of their earlier papers referring to ferroxidase...
Not citing your own earlier papers is a big tell....

author: ValWood
body:
This is a nice paper thorough 2010 paper from Biochemistry:
https://pubs.acs.org/doi/pdf/10.1021/bi1013062?ref=article_openPDF

Abstract:
"Most researchers agree that frataxin functions in the biogenesis of Fe-S clusters, but its precise role in this process is unclear. Here we provide in vitro evidence that human frataxin binds to a Nfs1, Isd11, and Isu2 complex to generate the fourcomponent core machinery for Fe-S cluster biosynthesis. Frataxin binding dramatically changes the KM for
cysteine from 0.59 to 0.011 mM and the catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM) of the cysteine desulfurase from 25 to 7900 M-1 s -1. Oxidizing conditions diminish the levels of both complex formation and frataxin-based
activation, whereas ferrous iron further stimulates cysteine desulfurase activity. 

The group who proposed ferroxidase later proposed the "iron storage" hypothesis which was also refulted:

"In vivo studies support a role for the 14 kDa monomeric
Fxn in Fe-S cluster assembly (20, 21), possibly as an iron
chaperone. An iron detoxification and storage role has also been
proposed (22, 23) and refuted (24, 25). Recently, Pastore and coworkers provided evidence that the Escherichia coli Fxn homologue
functions as a negative regulator for Fe-S cluster assembly (26).
Such a function for eukaryotic Fxn is difficult to reconcile with
genetic and biochemical data, which suggest Fxn facilitates rather
than inhibits Fe-S cluster biosynthesis (12, 20, 21, 27, 28). Further
kinetic experiments that address the effect of human frataxin on
Fe-S cluster biosynthesis are required to resolve this issue"

Again ferroxidase is not mentioned at all, this idea appears to died out after 2006.

The activities are not incompatible, enven though they are against the current consensus"

Important real-world example: Frataxin

Frataxin is central to this debate:

Reported activities:

Weak ferroxidase

Iron chaperone for Fe–S assembly

Current consensus:

Frataxin is not a classical ferroxidase

Any oxidation likely serves iron buffering or detoxification, not storage

Its role in Fe–S biogenesis is regulatory and iron-delivery–adjacent, not incompatible

This shows that low-level or conditional ferroxidase activity does not exclude Fe–S involvement.
